Washington, D. C.

All righty. Now let's begin at the beginning. Today we're interviewing Happy Caldwell. Your real name is Albert, right?
Right.
How did you get that nickname, first of all?

Well, as a matter of fact, I was a kid hanging around the garage a half a block from where I lived, and I always used to look out for (unintelligible) cars, and so I learned to drive a car without any instruction. Soon as the guy would get out, I'd take it, you know. Said, where your kid going with the car? Going around the block and come back. He said, oh, my goodness.
(Laughter)
So he said, well, never could discourage him, so the fellow that had the garage, name was -- he was a violin player and arranger, and he said, well, we're going to name him Happy, and the name stuck.
Yeah. Maybe because you got a happy disposition.
Well, I always had a -- I always liked to play a little on the happy side of life. Right, you know.
Well, are either of your parents

Well, I had two sisters. The oldest sister, (unintelligible) L. I The youngest sister was a great friend of Nell Armstrong before she married Louie, and they would come to the house, and my mother would have a beautiful piano because my youngest sister was taking music lessons. But the oldest sister never taken a lesson, so Lil and older sister'd come by and played, and so they get up behind them (unintelligible) and play. So Nell says, well, Josephine, why don't you take lessons? Don't have no time. But she had the better touch than my youngest sister. My youngest sister had a teacher come there to teach her, and oldest sister, Liddy Bowman come down and teach her, but she never acquired caught the taste.
But with me, I would -- I'd say I like the clarinet.
Yeah, but I mean did your father or mother every play an instrument?
My old man used to play fool with the banjo.
Oh, but then how come that -- how many were in your family?
Seven.
What were they then?
There's three girls and four boys. I'm the youngest of the family.
And did any of the others become professional musicians?
No.
Well, but nevertheless you had this piano home.
Yeah, I had the piano home.
Yeah, did you ever try playing that yourself?
The piano? I studied (unintelligible) chords on it, and I was taking some lessons, but I always liked the clarinet. I used to follow the band when we was at -- when -- they had the parade?
Yes.
I'd be right by the clarinet section, me and Omer Simcon and friend of -- we came up together on the clarinet, and we was going to listen to the clarinet. We didn't care about the other --
When did Elmer Simcon come up from New Orleans?
Simcon came back there because him and his brother went to school there, and they came up -- must have been in the early years because this was around 1922 and '21. We were going to high school.
Oh, I see. Where? Wendell Phillips?
That's where I went to, Wendell
Phillips.
And Omer went there too?
That's right.
Well, you know --
Cecil Erwin --
Well, I mean that was -- more people came out of that school than --
That's true. Milt Hinton (Unintelligible) and Hampton, bunch of them came out of that school.
And Nat Cole come out of there?
Yeah, because Nat, you know, when Hamp was going -- was there drumming, he went in -- I went into the National Guard band --
But wait a minute. We -- just -- we better not jump too much. When you -- when did you first begin to play clarinet?
In the high school band.
Oh, at the high school.
Yes, that's right.
Who taught you there?
Old man Tulesty started me off. He was the professor -- the conductor. But I finished up --
Well, how do you spell that?
Well, that's a German name, Tulesty, I think T-u-l-e-s-t-y, Tulesty.
Oh, I see.
Because that's the head man of the school, he was named German, descending the wife, the son, and then Buster -- I went with Buster.
Now, Buster in the book it says (unintelligible), he was a cousin of yours.
Right, distant cousin of mine, and I went with him because he was working with Erskine Tate at the Vendome Theater, and I used to go down there, and he would come over and take lessons.
Well, was Buster about the same age as you?
I think I'm a little older than Buster.
I see. But he had tuition on clarinet.
Oh, yes.
That was in Memphis.
Indeed -- that's right. But when he was a kid, he used to [play regular] out there before I did.
I think we started talking about Buster. We ought to mention the fact we're talking about Buster Bailey.
Right.
Yes, so he really helped you --
He did.
-- in addition to the school.

He really did. Yeah, I appreciate it. Funny thing about it, though, it was -- he was working with -- with this band down at the Sunset. So Simcan and I and Cecil Trwin Aaron, we all go and listen to the clarinet players, like Jimmy Noon, Buster Bailey and the different ones, you know. So Buster used to play this thing called Tod-Toot Tootsie Goodbye. Once he had -- I got it -- so bring him down to the Sunset, went in there, man, couple of guys, young fellows, and said, hey, Happy, come on and sit down. So Buster wasn't there that night. So I -- Rudy Jackson saxophone player, said, all right, Happy, said, come on and sit down. So I went and sat in -- so he played his thing, 'Tod-Toot Tootsie,' Goodbye.

I played the solo, exactly like in fact, Buster Bailey, said so Rudy said to me soon as he got set to leave, he said, 'hey, where did you get that like that?' I said 'because, I heard Buster play it over here a that note-for- couple times.' He said, 'how did you get all them multiple notes?' They went to (unintelligible) player said, 'oh, you're a copycat, huh?' And I said, 'no, I just like the way he played it did him all the good in the world, it.' He laughed and (unintelligible).
Which band was that then at -- Carroll
That was Carl Dickerson -- Carl Dickerson, uh-huh.
Yeah. Yeah.
Carl Dickerson. They had some great bands (unintelligible). in Chicago at that time.
So really Omar Simeon Elmer Simeon, he wasn't a clarinet player when he came from New Orleans.
No, I think he started in Chicago.
Yes.
Because his brother used to play the violin. I think they both -- I think they came when they were young kids.
What was the brother's name?
Oh, his name was Al.
Al, yes.

Very quiet fellow. Both of them Simeons are play, Simeon, a very beautiful fellows. We used to hang out at the -- we clarinet players -- every night we could, we'd put on long pants and go in the cabaret, like the Royal Garden, where Joe Oliver was Earl Gardner, Oliver Willis and like Jimmy Noonan and Ed Beckstrom. Dave Brady had the band at the Dreamland. We used to go to all of them -- (unintelligible) fellows. learn from all those
Yeah. Well, I mean the thing is at that time that you're talking of the kind of jazz people in Chicago were influenced very much by these guys from Chicago, from and New Orleans.
That's true.
: Yeah.

Then they had -- you know, the that too, started - actually their tunes, (unintelligible) -- I've met so many people come from different parts of the country that could play, like -- well, say like St. Louis and then Louisville, Kentucky -- and they had a style around Chicago, style was the one that impressed me for clarinet playing (unintelligible) Darnell gible) was Darnell Howard. Now, I didn't know that Darnell Howard and Benny Carter was cousins until I read it in John Chilton's book, John Chilton's book.
: Well, was Darnell born in Chicago?
I bet he was. I never knew that him and Benny was any relation.
: I never knew that either.
I got to write Benny and ask about that. (unintelligible). Benny and I were pretty close friends, but I never (unintelligible) --
: He was born in Chicago, 1895, Darnell
Darnell?
: Yeah. (Unintelligible).
Yes, I didn't know (he was) Benny Carter's was (unintelligible) cousin.

Well, is this John Chilton's book? Well, he got it in there. I think it's on Benny Carter or about either it's on (unintelligible) Darnell Howard. I would, might even get this (unintelligible) Benny was confirmed.
Yeah, that's right. It says Cuban Bennett and Dornell Howard was also Benny's -- yeah, that's interesting. Never heard that before.
I didn't either (unintelligible). I was over in Denmark and gave me the book. I never noticed it.
Yeah, he's got a lot of things in there. There's quite a few (unintelligible). (mistakes he found)
Yes, he did, and I was very surprised when I read it. Yeah, because I've read so many of them books. I went to Storyville
(unintelligible) story, though --
When were you -- now, when you went in this Army band, what was that? I mean --
That was the 370th Eighth Illinois (unintelligible) infantry National Guard band. And some of us fellows. And Dornell Howard was in that band too.
Well, you didn't -- I mean this wasn't like the real Army. This was the National Guard.
National Guard, yes.
I see. So you didn't leave Chicago with (unintelligible).
No, stationed in Chicago.
Yeah, I see.
Because when I was reading that, I thought, well, you'd be much too young.
That's true.
What were you, about 16 then?
We all fellas- (Unintelligible)

That's right. Yeah. was we all started to -- say, let's go enlist into the National Guard and get some good, you know, -- learning they were the playing that the Chicago ones played all type of music. So Hamp -- they had a-(unintelligible) with the colored publication, paper there. Hamp, Defender he went in to the Chicago Defender band, and we went into the Eighth Illinois North Infantry Band.
They were both marching bands.
Both marching bands.
Yeah, I see.
We young fellows, you know.
Yeah, but you got good tuition, though.
Oh, very good tuition played all the (unintelligible) big symphonics, big overtures, and then you played them big band marches, and then you played the concerts too.

Yeah, well this is where, I take it, that in some respects a city like Chicago or New York, you'd be a bit ahead of musicians coming from other parts of the country because they -- many of those early players couldn't read at all.
That's true, very true.
Yeah. And then when all those theaters are going in Chicago, and you got to read for them.
Yes, you got to read.
Yeah. Well, was that job with Young's band then your first professional job, or had you worked with anybody before that?

I'd worked with -- well, this little group out -- just out of Chicago called Indiana, which is still part of the city of Chicago, but East Chicago, and that is going into like East Chicago. You know, that's where a lot of the -- lot of baseball players came out of, and some athletes like prize fighters. It's on the outskirts.
Oh, it is part of Chicago.

Yeah. (Unintelligible) played night gigs, holidays, four, five of us, we'd go out there on the Illinois Central train, just a suburban train, about 40 minutes ride, and we'd play the job. We'd play on the train probably coming back. We'd pass the hat. We didn't mind.
Well, what sort of -- now, what time are we talking of now?
This was in -- this was around in '22 and '20 -- '22 and '23.
Well, were you playing jazz then?
Yeah, strictly jazz, trumpet, trombone, clarinet. I was thinking of clarinet playing.
Yeah, he's got 1922 -- joined Bernie Young's band in Columbia Tavern, Chicago.
Yeah, that's right, 31st and State Street.
31st and State? That's when Louis

Yeah. (Unintelligible) used to come by out there and stop. He was crazy about that little five piece group we had, and on his way over (unintelligible) moved to the -- Uncle Joe Oliver whatchacallit, (unintelligible) a job, he'd always stop in to hear these there when we used five pieces and say, okay, Pops. We never called him Pops them. We called him Louie. I was there when Louie first get off the boat, you know, when he came from -- Cuesth and Fate left Charlie (unintelligible) in Big Marable, and he came down, and Louie always was a very fine fellow.
Well, who else was in this band with you?

Bernie Young? Well, there's -- before he started out on guitar -- in fact he started out on the ukelele, and he used to tune his guitar up as a ukelele. We made him stop that and let him tune it up the way it should be. It was Mike McKendrick.
Oh, yeah.
See? And we started, Mike out. And there was -- Dolly's mother played trumpet.
What was her name?
Oh, let's see. What was Dolly's mother's name? Oh, I don't know. Her uncle played drums.
His Turk The name was (unintelligible).
What was Dolly's name?
Oh, my goodness. We had that didn't we?
(unintelligible)

Sure did, and (unintelligible) Dolly, all we know, you know the (unintelligible) the surname, All we did know was -- forget about it. We'd know the nickname. We always called her Dolly. (unintelligible) remember what that is? he
Is Dolly still alive?
No, he died. I bet you'd be surprised to know who her father is.
Her father is? Oh.
Yeah, did you ever read about him?
No.
One of the fellows that (unintelligible) played so much guitar, blues singer.
Lannie Bobby Johnson.
Right.
That was her father.
That was her father.
But she didn't take his name.
She didn't take his name.
I see.
That was news to me. Yeah, that was her father (unintelligible).
Well then, did her mother -- was her mother separated from -- you know in the show business
I guess (unintelligible).
Or did she marry after that? Yes.

She might have married a man after, you know how (unintelligible) show business is. Sometimes, you know, things like that happen just right, like with Jelly Roll. His wrote wife road after I was in California, and when Jelly Roll left New York (unintelligible) made these (unintelligible) recordings with him, he took his car and drove to California because his wife, his rich wife had a hotel out there, and this girl that was with him up to the time, years on the stage and all, she wasn't married to Jelly Charlie.
No. No. No, well, that was just the result of an affair.
That's right.
Yeah, I see. Yeah, well that's -- yes. But -- so it was Dolly's mother, though, that was playing trumpet.
Dolly's mother, right. Dolly used to come in and sit in.
Dolly did?

Her mother was a good reader too, because she played with those shows and circus too, and her uncle, called him Turk, he was (unintelligible) used to play at the old Monogram Theater had all these colored acts, and you had to
read all that stuff. Oh, he was a very good reader.
And then Bernie Young played trumpet himself.
Bernie, he organized, he took us out of that group and organized his own band for recording and playing. I left then.. I left that group at the Tavern and joined Bernie Young.
Wait a minute. What am I saying here? Well, whose was the band at the Tavern?
That blew it (unintelligible), the band actually belonged to -- the name was Dyer, they called him, real name was Dyer, Dolly's mother, Dyer Jones.
Dolly Jones, that's right.
That's right, was Dyer Jones -- her name was Dolly Jones. She had the group.
Oh, she was the leader.

She had the group, and then when she left, then we turned it over, had a fellow named Wilson, was a very good trumpet player, young fellow. We all was young. Then we got a drummer from Louisville named Burton because Bobby Williams was working with -- with the -- at the Sunset with Cat Correll Dickerson, with -- beautiful trumpet player. Bobby, his name was in that book, but when you ever heard him play, Roy Eldridge (unintelligible) was just a replica of what Bobby Williams was.
Really?
That's right.
Oh, that's interesting. (Unintelligible). I mean this was very early, isn't it? he was a
Yeah, but (unintelligible) wonderful trumpet player, always execution.
Well, what happened to him?

He got with the -- funny thing about that, I think he ate something with poison that sit back on him. He was a fine fellow, very fine fellow. Only, you know, thing about those fellows, when we were kids, young guys coming up, they always liked to see us make progress. They say, when you got to the folks you can play something. Well, what do you want to play? We say, oh, we play so and so, so (Simon and and so. All right. We go in there, sit in and play, myself and Cecil Irwin.

And when we graduated from grammar school and from high school, we were always supposed to go to Atlanta, Georgia, to go to the Morehouse University because they had a big, beautiful -- they had a mixed curriculum there for students. And he went to Morehouse, and I went to Wilberforce. So they could --
Cecil went to Morehouse?
Yeah, Cecil Irwin (unintelligible) went to Morehouse, and I went to Wilberforce -- Wilberforce University.
Why was that?

Well, we all had decided to go one place together, but then, you know, parents, they have something to do with where you're going to go anyway, so when we finished high school, he went to Morehouse, and I went to Wilberforce.
Well, I mean he -- Cecil Irwin, he must have got -- I mean he was really very advanced, wasn't he, as an arranger and everything?
Yeah, was a very fine clarinet player, just same as Simon (unintelligible) because we all stuck, the three guys, we three just -- one without the other. We all just stuck together.
Were you all playing Albert (unintelligible) system in those days?
Always played Albert system.
Yeah.
And eventually, when I went into the Army band -- the National Guard, then you had a choice of switching over to the Boehm system.
Well, which did you like?

Well, actually the Boehm system was more for -- more like execution, but I just liked the Albert system because a fellow (practically) gave me the Albert system -- the A clarinet and the B flat clarinet, and we then proved
the Albert system. They got -- they're beautiful. They got some beautiful -- but you could make a lot of free passages on the Albert that you couldn't make on the Boehm system.

That's right. Were -- you know, it's a funny thing how some people want to say that there's really, you know, anything you can play on the Boehm system you can play on the Albert and vice versa, but there's a difference. It's a difference.
It's a difference.
There is.
Certainly is.
Benny Goodman told me that.
That's right. He's right.
There were some things that you could do on the Albert (unintelligible) that you could not do on Boehm (unintelligible).
That's true, very true.
And it always seemed to (unintelligible) the people that played the Albert somehow. I don't know why they should, but it always seemed that there was a difference of tone.
It was.
Well, why was that?
The -- I think what it is, Stanley, is that the construction of the instrument is different because

everything -- once you get the swing of it, you can find so many funny notes you want to make. Not only lipping (unintelligible) but the Johnny Dodds fingering too -- I used to make a whole lot like tiny dots.

When I got my first saxophone was -- it was an alto -- I taken it to Johnny he Joe Oliver (unintelligible) at the -- where you worked with (unintelligible). I said, Johnny, want me to play the saxophone? "Well Happy what "Well my parents He'd say, what the hell you going to do with it. So I bought it for me but no saxophone (unintelligible) I don't like (unintelligible) because we guys were clarinet bugs, you know?
Right.

MR. CALDWELL: And Johnny (unintelligible) taken it and he'd play it for about two months, say, you come on and get your saxophone. I said, all right, but, I said, I thought you were going to play the thing. It still wasn't played. But (by) that time I was ready to there moderator could leave Chicago and go to New York. So I'd taken my old horn -- it was a good horn -- and left it was getting with Mamie home. I (back) (unintelligible) coming to New York. Mamie But (unintelligible) interested in the clarinet.

Then Hawk came through before I left with Mamie, slap tonguing and I got stuck playing with the tenor. Hawk was (unin- telligible). He was crazy about my clarinet style. I said-- he said to me, said, hey, say, why don't you come on and join us? I said, well, Hawk --
Is this when you first met him?
First met him, yeah, when I first
met Hawk.
Was he -- I mean when you first heard him, was he still playing the 'cello?
You know, he learned 'cello there in Chicago University in music. He studied there in Chicago for a while.
He did?
Yes, he did.

Well, you know that a funny thing -- I think it was when Harry Carney died. I was at that funeral home when the first person (unintelligible) -- well, he's a sax -- an old saxophone player. Lives We used to go out in Long Island. And I was talking to him, and he said, I remember Hawk playing 'cello with Raymond Smith.
He could play cello. He used to double on cello.
Did you ever see him play it?
Sure.
You did?
Yeah. And we --
(Simultaneous remarks)
Did he just play sort of straight? I mean --
Boy, he went to school on it, and he played it first after he studied at the University of --

Chicago University of Music, and he learned -- his instrument was cello, piano and cello. No, he could arrange them when But Hawk sometimes was a little lazy he wanted to. (Unintelligible), you know, and he could play a good clarinet. Lot of people didn't know that, but he could.
But he just laid it down.
He just didn't want to bother with it.
Yeah.

I said, Bean -- we used to call him Bean for short -- if we could call him -- well, I always called him Hawk. I said, "hey Bean" (unintelligible), why don't you play the clarinet?" He said, "that's why I asked you to join us when I met you in Chicago. He said, we liked your style because you was swinging with the clarinet." So I was doubling on — . Mainly I was doubling from the alto to the tenor and -- but we got in New York, and I sort of worked with from alto Benny. And I stayed on alto and then switched to baritone and tenor. So I got tired of switching from one instrument to the other, so I said, well, I'm not going to switch back, alto because Cab wanted me on also. I said, no, I'm not (unintelligible) down at the Nest Club working with fellows, you know, names that you all know, said, I'm going to stay on tenor.
Well, when you -- when you -- now, just when -- when you went with Bernie Young back, didn't you go to
Wisconsin or something?
Went to Wisconsin.
How long did you play there?
I played there for about six months. I came back to the Wisconsin Roof Garden. When I came back --
Yeah. Roof garden on a hotel?
It was a hotel, yeah.
That must have been a fairly good job for those days.

Yes, it was. We stayed there for about, oh, I think about four or five years. They sent for me when I was in New Jersey working in Newark, and they sent for me (unintelligible) but I'm doing good and liked the East too (unintelligible) and living in New York and working over in Newark. Rex Stewart and myself, we were good buddies, Walter Johnson (unintelligible) going.
Well, when you -- just back to that record. You did record (unintelligible) in '23. with Bernie Young (unintelligible) then) (unintelligible)
'23. First I (unintelligible) we started with because we skipped (unintelligible), but Bernie Young on Mike McKendrick trumpet, Mack Hendricks on guitar, Preston Jackson on trombone.
Casino? [Cassino]
I played clarinet. He went to New Orleans last year to live.
Who?
Preston Jackson did.
Oh, yeah?

He got a lot of work there. That's his home, you know. But he was raised up in Chicago. And Stump Evans. See, Stump was a trombone player and a saxophone player. He was from out of St. Joe -- out of Kansas City, Missouri.
But what instrument -- what was he playing, alto or tenor?
He was playing alto. No, he was playing, c- melody.
Oh.
Or that (Unintelligible) recording. I played on the -- strictly clarinet.
Yeah.

But a lot of people didn't know that Stump -- even Hawk didn't know it, until Hawk -- until I ran into Hawk one day up there in the Masonic temple, and he said to me, he said, Hap, I want to ask you a question. I said, what you want, Bean? I said, anything. I never heard Stump, but I heard him, you know, from records, said, what kind of fellow was he? I said, Hawk, if he'd come here like we do anything, you know, that you asked him to, said, he'd upset everybody like you did. He said, well, what else did he play? I said, trombone and c-melody (Unintelligible).
Yeah. But then he went to tenor.
Then he went to tenor. When we sent for him to come to New York, Cab wanted to --
You know, think it was Earl Hines told me that when -- (at the Sunset) -- he was in that band?
Yeah.
Well, he said, you know, he kept telling -- great tenor player! I said, no, the man played -- I thought he played the alto. No, he said, tenor.
Well, he -- a lot of people might think (unintelligible) trombone. 'cause his horn was C-melody and
Yeah.
But on this recording we made with Bernie, you know, he's on (unintelligible) C-melody.
Yeah. Yeah. Lots of people would think that's an alto.
Yes, well, they would. It's the tone, you know, so similar. I used to play (unintelligible) C-melody, and Benny Carter did too.
Well, why did that instrument get dropped? Because that had a certain -- I mean like what was that, Frankie Trumbauer (unintelligible).
Yeah.
Now, I mean he did things on there which were very individual.
Very individual. Now, Frankie and

I was good friends. He used to tell me, said, you were on alto, said, why did you go back to tenor? I said, I like the tenor better. He said, stay on it. And Hawk always told me, he says, look, says, you got -- one thing about it I like about you. You don't let nobody influence you. He said, you got your own way of doing things. I said, well, Hawk, I learned that. Just part of me, I said, I love everybody's playing, but I won't let their influence just -- like in later years in New York when bebop came in, once you hear one wind instrument playing a solo, you almost hear all the other instruments because everybody's (unintelligible). But --
(unintelligible)
is this
: But, you know, the thing (unintelligible) some of those people that began on alto and switched to tenor --
That's right.
: -- now, they -- I mean like Lester Young.
Now, you know, you think, well this guy really might just as well be playing alto (unintelligible) --
That's true; that's right.
-- because he's not sort of producing all the tone that the tenor can produce.
That's right.
: But I suppose to some extent if you
played the alto first, it would sort of affect your ear and the way you play the other instruments.

Really would, because I used to double for -- from the B flat tenor to the E flat baritone saxophone, like with Arthur Gibbs band. And Benny Carter (said, you play) alto wanted -- fine also. I could pick up the alto and play it. you an unshy fellow, and I said why He said (unintelligible), said, you play the tenor and you turn around, just pick up the alto out of the clear blue sky, and you play it. I said, you know, everybody -- sometimes return people just got the knack or the ability some way, just like I used to pick up the clarinet. I don't have anything in over ten, 11 or 12 years. I got two of them. I gave one away. Still got two more. a lot of time Lot of bands went out of town, said, you came up in the era -- in the era when the Dixieland and all clarinet, why don't you that jazz on (unintelligible) wanted to go back on clarinet.
Well, I was thinking the same thing. You know, it's a funny thing that -- well, how much would it take you to sort of pick up the clarinet and work on it?
Oh, I think about four months.

So I mean you -- I know sometimes after the -- after the people have reached, become the worshipful master, then they rather lose interest.

Some of them do. In fact, some of them never come back. Now, this -- lotte time -- all these fellows have passed (unintelligible) worshipful mastership, whenever we have any committee meetings and communication night, you see more past masters than you see almost the (unintelligible) officer. So I always get up and tell them, I says, look, all you appointed officers, you elected officers, I say, you have a duty to perform. So now, if you expect to go anywhere, I said, because the highest honor is becoming master for the lodge, said, you [run] across a white mason, and he's a big man in his fraternity, masonic fraternity, and you get to talking, the first (unintelligible) you tell him where you travel and how far you went, when you said you're a master, he know you have worked, because there's no honorary master, no honorary past master.

You can get the honorary past potentate degree, see, but you can't no past -- get no past master degree. You got to work for that. Same as in the Royal Arch Chapter. You can't get no honorary past high priest. I'm a past high priest in my Royal Arch Chapter, which is the oldest, and historian too, and I'm chairman of the trustee board.
Well now, how does this -- in the
music business, do you think one brother helps another when he can?
Yeah, he sure does.
I mean -- I mean suppose for the sake of argument you were putting a band together, and there were two trombone players equally good, would you take the brother rather than the non --
If he was a brother that I know didn't adhere to the principles of doing what he's supposed to do --
Oh, you wouldn't.
I'd take the other man.
Right. But I mean assuming that he's -- I mean in a way if you had the opportunity to favor a member of your lodge who was a -- you would do it?
Yes.
Well, that's what you're supposed to do.
(Simultaneous remarks)
Well, actually, I mean it gives you something in your -- you know, my father always claimed that if you lived up to it, you really didn't have to go to church.
It's true, because (unintelligible) in order with when you take the solemn obligation, you have to be the old man above.
You sure did.

You had to be in with him. Otherwise, that's the finish of that. And if he don't go to church, even with all the houses that he belong to, blue house, red house, the consistory or the knights of templars or the Shrines, everyone have a divine service, and that's -- you got to go to church five times a year if you never go at all if you're going to be a -- you know --
Well, I mean, you know, I mean quite apart from the kind of ritual of it, the moral --
(Simultaneous remarks)
That's true.
In other words, I mean you -- you really -- you're sort of confirming the fact that you don't believe in cheating, robbing --
That's true.
-- lying -- I mean, you know—
(Simultaneous remarks)
It's a good thing.
It's a good thing.
That's right.
You know, actually, Stanley, when you --
It's not like a Rotary Club, where -- you know, I mean a Rotary Club is a backslapping thing,
try to benefit each other, but that's a business thing.
Well, you will find a devil in all organizations.
Oh, sure.

And consequently -- but when you -- after you realize -- you get into it, you find out it's everyday life. You find a lot of people never belong to anything but just as conscientious toward (unintelligible) to your fellow man, and then when he gets in, he find out the precepts where he's at home. He says, well, this I've been doing all my life. Now I understand what it means. So he's a good man.
I -- I mean the three or four masonic funerals I've seen uptown have been very well done and very impressively done.
Yeah, they is only about one hour long. Now, it's only about one hour.
Yeah, but I mean they've been very well conducted, with dignity, because, after all, you know, you can -- with the best will in the world (unintelligible) you could goof up in (unintelligible).
That's true.
You know, I mean--
Very much.
I mean you could learn all that stuff, but you're still going to slip up, get nervous (unintelligible), --
That's true. That's right.
-- but they're very well done.

Very well. They have a regular what you call team for -- to substitute anytime they do funeral [two times.] Between Kenneth Roane- he's past master (unintelligible) Dial, he's past master, he would do the funeral (table). We would do the other parts with him. And one time we had funerals back to back. Had to and do one on a Monday, me on a Tuesday. We had -- that year, in 1959, we had 11 funerals. And we had to participate in all those funerals. So between Harry Dial and Lem Johnson they'll alternate (unintelligible) doing Roane these funerals, because and I, we were stuck with the warden's part, so we just did the part that's -- every time they had a (unintelligible) the funeral, 11 of them that year. I only had one funeral when I was a master. I was very lucky.

You know, the thing that strikes me as funny, when you come to think of it, is all that business of the New Orleans funerals, marching out and playing, the band playing back. Now, you know, they've made a sort of a gimmick of that really.
Yes, it did.
I don't -- in a way that's a kind of mockery.
It is, true. We was [crossed out] there.

"Didn't he they do Ramble." They It's kind of a mockery because it's -- used to play that thing coming back from the funeral-- the "Free as the cemetery, (unintelligible) birds", like that, you know, because we used to -- years ago in New York, had like the big person was -- had died, like Mason or Odd- fellows. They don't have those funerals up and down the streets anymore in New York like they did years ago. They don't have them anymore. Mostly they do the thing at the temple or at the big funeral parlor. Even whites don't have that much like they used to.

Yeah, well, there's a funny thing about that. I mean there is the New Orleans thing, and then there is like some of the funeral services they have in churches here, where people get up -- I mean you've been to some of them, and they sing and they play, and it's almost as though they were doing an audition.
Yeah, that's true.
You know, I mean that service for Ray Nance, did you go to that?

I missed Ray Nance -- you know, I didn't know Ray Nance had died until somebody called me on the contemplating Milt Hinton phone, and I was (unintelligible) and this regular Chicago bunch from the south side. The fellow in Denmark said, Hap, all those they get out-of Chicago's together. I said, yeah, I says, and I thought it was -- was whatchacallum.
Well, that funeral service went on for over two hours.
Oh, no.
(Simultaneous remarks)
Pastor Gense. Ray's wife --

Yes, that was his wife. She asked for me to deliver the eulogy because I knew (unintelligible). Well, so when I get there, you know, I'd sort of written out something, not too long, Pastor Gense (unintelligible) had George Wein get up and deliver a sort of eulogy. Then he -- then I think someone in the middle of this thing -- I had to get up. Now, George Wein has already said some of the things I was going to say. It put me in a foolish position.

And then after I'd finished, after about a quarter of an hour of it, he reads out a sort of a eulogy that a priest in Montreal who knew Ray Nance (unintelligible), read this out. And in between we have girls singing, reading poems they had written and guys singing, and then -- I mean this went on for over two hours, and I think that's ridiculous. If anybody is seriously grieving for him, I mean you don't want to have to sit in that church for two hours. His mother was there. I mean how would she feel?

I know, I mean that's why I've been to those things masonic temples which have sort of done -- I mean Red Allen's funeral, which was a straight Catholic mass -- I mean to me that seemed right, but I don't particularly go for making a
vaudeville show out of it.
I don't either. Fine
I mean I think (unintelligible) to have somebody playing My Buddy and so forth at the end. I think that's very nice.
Yes, it is.
But I don't think you need about six or seven different acts.
No, no, definitely not. I know like at Zooty's funeral -- I forgot the trombone player's name, Milt Hampton, and they played a couple numbers. That was enough.
(Simultaneous remarks)
Now, wait -- you've got to -- I mean what have you been doing in recent years. We've got to cover that too.
Oh, soon as I came back from -- well, --
I mean you -- we were talking about you going into masonry in '46. Now, you've -- from that time on, I take it, you were playing around New York.
Definitely, yeah.
Were you playing with your own groups as a side man?
No, I played both -- then I've worked

with guys who get stuck. They call me. A lot of guys I (unintelligible) think I couldn't play with them because I was being with groups of my own. I said, no, you're stuck. I'll be with you. (Go, or why) (unintelligible) -- I was playing a side man.

Yes, quite often, yes.

Yeah.

When did you start this?
That was 19- -- I believe that's November, 1957.
And what did you do? What do you do?

Well, first it was in the mail room. Then (being) (unintelligible) worked in the post office (before) (unintelligible) it was easy for me, but then this (unintelligible) we'll show you how to operate these machines. So I learned it fast,

and I instituted something over there that wasn't done before. Well, they say, well, I've always been doing it this way. Well, I say, that's the wrong way.

You do it this way. So they (unintelligible), said, well, how (unintelligible). I say, there's a diagram in the stencil. It's a square. That's where you use it from that, postal card, any size card. seminars (crossed out: little jazz, something about it), kids would come up, you know.

: Yeah, well, maybe so --

: He did -- well, what does he do for
work?

is he?

(Unintelligible) Gene about -- oh, I guess almost 15 years I ran into him around Doc Vollmer's there. He was -- when I looked at him --

Tommy -- I would take (unintelligible) bass, couldn't get George Dupvier, (unintelligible) but I'd take this other fellow there plays very good guitar and bass, and he does these things around these different colleges, writes and arranges, and he's got a well known name too in music.

His name is Wilson. I don't think he ever made the big top, but he's very good. He's always working.
Gene Rodgers, right, New York City.
Is that Gene Rodgers? Yeah, New York City.
Yeah. Well, then -- say, you go down and you play. And then what else?
You play and then students ask little questions. (unintelligible) certain (unintelligible).
Do you with each -- I mean if they want to know something about the piano, does Gene --
Yeah.
I see.

They are.
You know, they have some good bands too there.

-- Doc Cheatham and people like that.
That would be the same sort of thing.
Same thing.

Still making gigs, working on that part time anyway.
Well, one thing, you know, we never mentioned, but during that time you were in Philadelphia, you became a journalist and wrote a column in a New York magazine called Music Dial.
That's true.
How long did you do that?

Well, I did that -- that happened in '43 to '44, and I came back here, moved back to New York in about November of '44. Then I stayed because I was going over, commuting for being the dean on the executive board of Local #274, elected.
Oh, in Philly?
In Philly, yeah. Yeah, I was elected executive board member.
Well, how long were you on that?
Two years.
Yeah?
Uh-huh.
Have you ever done anything with this union in New York?
No, and I could have been appointed as a delegate, but I wouldn't take it now because since (Unintelligible) -- Jack Wilson died here about a month and a half ago. I wasn't going to bother with it.
No. Well, you know, that's —
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- about 13 or 20 years ago it was a little bit different, but I was doing so much gig work, playing for different clubs and fraternity -- for the fraternity and then working on my day job too, so --
Yeah. What was your day job?
I work for City College.
Oh, the City College job, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, well, I mean you've done -- really kept very active then.
Yeah, very active. See, between that and the lodge too, so --
Yeah. Well, I mean (unintelligible) it's very important too, isn't it?
Yeah, very nice.
You know, all the nights you were -- I mean if you just sat at home.
Oh, no.
You -- that's not good, is it?
No good.

Well now, we've just got to recap a bit now on this last half hour. It seems to me that we did get out of Chicago a little bit quick. You did speak about -- but, of course, you -- yeah, you really left Chicago before it -- I mean you left Chicago so damn early, didn't you?
Yeah, February, 1924.
(Laughter)
A lot happened in Chicago.

Yeah, it did. Since I left Chicago, yes, it did. I was there this past December visiting my (owns a house there) niece, nephew and my sister (unintelligible) South Chicago Avenue, stayed there a week, because I came there --
What time of year did you go there?
This past December.
Oh, well, that's not -- that wasn't too bad, but if you have to go there in the realy wintry weather, I don't know how people stand that place.
Well, I tell you the truth. When I left there with Mamie Smith in February of 1924, it was so cold you couldn't see out of the taxicab windows (going out to the train station (unintelligible)).
Oh, I believe it. I mean --
Couldn't see.
-- you walk along, you turn a street corner, and the tears come out of your eyes.
That's it.
-- you can't -- oh, I think that's an awful place. The winter --
That's why they call it the Windy city.
That's a rough place.
Rough place, right off that Lake Michigan.
And that must have been very rough, well, really the gangster days hadn't begun when you left.

They were just beginning because I was working downtown during my vacation off from high school when this guy, Big Jim Collinsimo, had a place down on Wabash Avenue and I think it was around 23rd Street -- Big Jim Colisemo. Old Eddie South Softan worked a lot of them, worked there, and when they got Al Capone from Brooklyn here, that's where the seat of the Mafia was started there, because Big Jim Colisimo was Italian, and they moved in there. That's when Capone came from New York, Brooklyn to Chicago.

Now Frankie Yale was the leader to the Capones, but he never got along too good a little, and that's when this thing started in Chicago, and going home one afternoon here I seen all these patrol wagons out there on State Street, all way back on Wabash Avenue. Come to find out they assassinated Big Jim Colisemo. That was the beginning of it.
That was the beginning.
That was the beginning.
Yeah. Well, of course, there's -- those -- although those were bad years from the night club point of view, they weren't really bad, were they?
No, they weren't really bad.
Not for the -- you know, the prohibition and all that nonsense. I mean as far as work for musicians was concerned, it didn't do anything, didn't do any harm.

No, didn't do any harm. No, because it's so -- of course, Chicago was so far ahead of New York at that time for night life because every corner you had a club, after hour joints, you know. Like, for instance—
Well, why was that?
Why was Chicago ahead of New York?
Well, at that particular time Chicago was cabaret center in this country because you --
(Side Ten)
Well, what we're really talking about here is Chicago, which was kind of unique, but the night life thing in Chicago in the South Side when you left in '24 -- is that right --
Yeah.
-- was far ahead of Harlem.
That's right.
Well now, what we're trying to do is account for why this was.
Well, first place --
Just excuse me for one second, Happy. Was there a bigger black population in Chicago then than in New York?
I think for night life, yes, it was, because --
I mean in total.
In total population you mean.
Well, I mean was the black population in Chicago bigger than New York?
I think so, particular time. I think so.
Yeah. Or maybe more concentrated.

Yeah, it was more concentrated, because most of it be outside of downtown, like the West Side in Chicago. Well, that was a different thing because they had a lot of smaller clubs over there. Where?
The Radio Inn.

Fiume? How do you spell that?
F-i-u-m-e. It's Italian city.
Oh, like the Italian city.

Right. That was after hours. And like going down to 31st Street, they had the Schiller's Inn, which was another nice offside cabaret; where we worked was at Columbia Tavern off 35th -- on 31st and State underneath the

Columbia Hotel. Then you had a place down further -- Jack Johnson used to own (unintelligible) to them. Well, there was a cabaret and after hours joint. Now, that's down in that part of the section. I see. Yeah.

Well, I just wondered whether it was a place that's different from all the orders and so forth used.

Yeah, well, it was -- that burned down practically. and it was rehabilitated and called it -- named the Vendome.. Up further on the street there was a lot of little movie houses on the way up, TOBA houses. Then big cabarets came in, then the movie houses, all the way out to, say, 47th Street and State; different ones had big bands in those houses.

-- when I was a kid.

(Recording interruption)
When you first heard him?
Chu was playing alto. Chu was working down at the Colonnades when I was down there with -- with Arthur Gibbs, and Fat Man Turner, the bass player, had taken the band into the Colonnades.
Well, he had a band called the Arcadians

Right. That's true. And I forgot who the tenor player was. Anyway, Chu was on alto. That's one of those things that happened, a coincidence, and the tenor player didn't show. So they requested -- we always used three saxophones, alto, two altos and a tenor. So the tenor man didn't show, so they had to substitute another alto. So Chu picked up the tenor because we leave the tenors -- at that time in those barrooms -- unprotected. You could leave them on the stand, right on the stand. When it comes to the break, you leave them on the stand right in there.
Really?
That's right.
Well, why was that? I mean --
They have a lot of guys didn't worry about taking them home or --
I mean was there better protection or something?
Sure, because they had guards. They
had guards there and a couple of guys there all night.
So Chu just picked up this --
We picked up the horn -- I'd just leave mine there too. And (unintelligible) it up, fill in, tenor player wasn't there that night. Chu Then Chu liked it. Chu stayed on it. That was it.
Well, in a way you might almost say, when you point that out, that you can partly hear that.
That's true.
You know? I mean that is -- there's something a little of the alto in that.
It is. Yeah, this is quite true.

But he was -- I mean he's another guy that is, you know, as the history of jazz lengthens, people like that get forgotten. You know, they say Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster, Lester Young, and then you -- you know, there's -- but I mean he was a great guy. I mean --
Yes, he was.
I mean that was a very distinctive style and --
Very.
He certainly was one of the swingingest ever.
That's right, he sure was.
Yeah.
Well, we played in Charleston, West Virginia. That's his home. And we were with Tiny. Bradshaw
Tiny

Uh-huh. So we said, well, we got a day off. Let's go down to the Elks' Home. So I said, okay, let's go to the Elks' Home, you know, you don't go there to buy ain't nothing just to go around have a ball. So we got down there and up against the wall behind the bar was Chu Berry's picture. So I told the bartender, I says, hey, that's Chu Berry. He said, you know him? I said, sure, I know him. But then you couldn't buy nothing.
(Laughter)
That was his home.
Yeah, I see.

He says, what do you play? I said, the saxophone. I remember Chu first came to New York. Said, what are you drinking? I said, a little gin and anisette. He said, you don't pay for nothing in here. That's the way it was. He was just loved. And that's Fat Man's home too, Charleston, West Virginia.
Did he come up with him? Did they come up together? I forget.
No, Fat Man came out of Charleston, went to Pennsylvania, went to Chicago. That's when he formed the Arcadians, came back to New York with the Arcadians.
Oh, I see.
Of course, he had quite a few Chicagoans in that band, see. And you couldn't buy nothing there in that Elk's home if you knew Chu Berry, especially (unintelligible).
Well, who do you think -- I mean now there's a good question. I mean who do you think Chu had to influence him? I mean by that time, I suppose, he must have heard Hawk.
Oh, well, all means, sure he heard Hawk. He heard Hawk before he heard Ben. we all heard Hawk was up before Ben.
Yeah, but earlier on you were talking about Hawk and Prince Robinson. Well, there was a time when that was Hawk and Prince Robinson were two of the best (unintelligible).

You had to get -- got to get by all three of us. That was the whole question, tough thing. They made it that way. Whenever Hawk and I would be playing, we wouldn't pay that no mind, but that was the proving grounds.
Well, now wait a minute. Prince was with McKinney's, right?
Well, he left. He went with McKinney's in later years.
Well, where was he making his name

He started, him and Bob Robertson, the one that sponsored me in masons, they were working with fellow named Bendy Howard, had a band on 140th Street and Lenox, called the Calvert Palace. It was a good band. It was eight pieces.
What was his name?

Bendy Howard. And that's when I -- they thought that Prince Robertson and Bob Robertson were brothers, but they weren't, because the both of them came out of Virginia. But they were no relation. And they had a fine band, a group, good band. And that was back, oh, that was around --
Well, I mean did Prince -- do you think -- I mean you yourself had heard Hawk.
Oh, by all means.
So you were influenced by him, naturally, since you had got a -- you were coming off clarinet onto tenor.
Right.
Well now, when -- what -- I mean do you think Prince was influenced by Hawk?
I think he was because he -- he was playing clarinet like I was. When he came to New York, he was playing then clarinet and tenor.
So really, I mean Hawk was like first with that tone.
Right. He was first of most of us fellows. He influenced most of us fellows, because --
But you know there was another tenor that I always used to think was good, never got mentioned much -- Bob Carroll. Do you remember him?
Bob Carroll, him and I were very good buddies.
He sounded good.

Now, he was a fine tenor player, but Bob -- I could do more with Bob, I guess, and Ben than anybody. They all liked me. They liked my style of playing. He had a peculiar way of playing, beautiful thing. He played, you know, interpretations. And one day we were rehearsing to go to the Apollo Theater. So they had (unintelligible) on bass. So Jesse Stone had did the arranging.
Who?
Jesse Jones -- Jesse Stone -- he the one that wrote 'Idaho'.
Yes, yes.

And he was very talented arranger, you know. So he would write parts like for the reeds, brass, like baritone, sax, bass and trombone, he would -- you know, he had that thing (unintelligible) with him. So we would

rehearse, were rehearsing. Bob was a character, really character, you know. We'd -- let the reed section run off our parts, and everything Jesse said (unintelligible) fine, and beautiful. So we'd lay the horns down. There's something wrong, some passages there, that bass and baritone sax and the trombones, he had a part played from the passages. So Bob was comical anyway, Bob. I said, what do you say, Bob? He said, huh, man, we've been here a whole three hours playing, practicing, rehearsing, and that cutback tone, that bass. I said, Bob, said, he'll get together later on. What? That (unintelligible) too, Bob. I said, let's go on out and get a little taste right around the Braddock there. We were rehearsing down in the Braddock Hotel.

So Bob started to talk, said, I'm going to straighten that son of a bitch out. I said, Bob, leave the man alone. Well, (unintelligible) came back, he said, fellows, we going to learn this (unintelligible) again. So Bob said, hey, Jesse, -- what do you want to do now? He said, same thing. Well, the saxophone section, we got ours, said, what's wrong with that passage (unintelligible), said, everybody playing it but the trombones and the baritone and the trombone, but the bass player ain't reading that. That started the argument.
So I'm trying to keep Bob quiet. That didn't do no good. I got to tell him, I said, Bob, don't pay no mind.

Why not tell him, man? I said, Bob, you going to start confusing (unintelligible). You don't start that foolishness. (UNintelligible). Hey, look, you take that part home and practice, because you ain't playing nothing on that music. Then Brand got mad. They broke up (unintelligible). Oh, Lord, they broke up the rehearsal. I walked, picked my knife out (unintelligible). Bob said, take the saxophone. I said, oh, boy.
(Laughter)
But that's the way Bob was. Bob Carroll, Ben Webster and Bob Dorsey --
Bob Dorsey?
Yeah, saxophone. He came there with -- with Hawk -- with Horace, with --
Nat Towles?
No, he came there with Fletcher and his brother brought him here, Horace Henderson.
Oh, Horace took some band members.
That's right. He booked him here.
Nat Towles -- no, Ernie Fields or something or other.

No, he was a good tenor player. Now, all around the same size, like Ben Webster. So one day I'm going up to the Apollo Theater, said, I'll stop at the bar and talk with the fellows in the performance. So I saw all this crowd stopping by (unintelligible) near the back end of the Apollo Theater

on 126th towards Sixth Street. So (unintelligible) said, say, Hap, one of the comedians Pigmeat said, come here. I said, hey, what do you say, (unintelligible). Why don't you go (unintelligible) them cats are? I said, about what? Who is it? Said, them three old B's. We called them the three B's -- Bob Dorsey, Ben Webster and --- I said, who? He said, the three B's up there. I said, oh, Lord, said, I ain't going to get in this.
What were they up to?

Probably about something, music or something. They got to arguing and been drinking, you know. Well, Wesley was -- wanted to get in a fight, but they were how musicians are, just, you know, it was just a joke. So I couldn't duck it. So when Ben Webster and them saw me and Bob Carroll, hey, Happy, Happy Caldwell, (unintelligible) straighten that out right now. Happy, come here. I said, oh, boy.
(Laughter and simultaneous remarks)

I said, what's -- what's wrong. Hap, Carroll -- this cat here is so and so and so and so. Then he got you to refresh your memory, go back because I was there before them fellows ever came to New York, talking about Hawk. So he said, if any man know Hawk. Ben said, it would be you. Said, now, we just keep quiet, just ask one question. That's it. What he said -- we'll take it. So I asked the question. It was right.
So Ben said, that's all I want to know. Bob Carroll said, I told you, you big bum, you.
(Laughter)
Talking to Bob Dorsey (unintelligible). He was -- he was -- he wanted fight the policeman wasn't trying to (unintelligible), but Bob was funny, and he had a good education.
Well, but he -- didn't he die. Wasn't he getting to be an alcoholic?

Yeah, he drank, and one day wewere out there on 132nd Street by the Rhythm Club, and there's a bar on the corner. So we go out there talking, and I went to the bar. We worked downstairs there. So Bob, he said, Happy, he said, come on out and get straight (unintelligible) and buy a bottle. I said, Bob, we'll get in trouble, said, what Bob? Bob Carroll. So I went out there with Bob (unintelligible) had him by the heck. guy anybody make. They were wrestling around all over Seventh Avenue.
I said, hey, Bob, said, get up before the police come and lock you guys, lock you up. Bob said, I got this son of a bitch down, Hap, and I'm going to whip him up good.
(Laughter)
I said, Bob, come on. Get up. I said, here come the policeman. I'm going to hold him (unintelligible). I'm going to whip him. I said, oh, no, this guy going to get put in jail.
How did he die, though?
He died -- they told me that, of course, Bob would drink, but he never was what you call a
alcoholic, but he just would drink enough to act foolish, raise hell.
Oh, I see, yeah.
Yeah, see.
He wasn't evil. He was just -- yeah.

No, just that way. (Unintelligible) saw the crowd, so the policeman come, and I said, Bob, if you don't get up from there, the man going to take you to your come on (unintelligible) now. Where's the (unintelligible)? I said, there up on 133rd Street. I'm going to whip this sucker again. I said, oh, man, said, would you come on? This is Happy talking to you. All right, Hap. Jumped up, kicked the came in all dirty Come on to the bar, guy. (unintelligible), man, come on. Bob (unintelligible). I said, get a drink right quick.
Did you find out what they were fighting about?
Nobody knew. I don't know what Bob -- Bob -- could have been something -- he would -- Bob would get full of that whiskey, he'd chew the policeman.
But I mean he -- I was trying to think whether it was with Don Redman's records. He sounded very good.
That was -- I loved his playing.
But I was thinking, now, if you take
that beginning. There's Hawk. There's you and Prince.
Right.
Now, okay, you're really like the first three, I reckon, aren't you?
Well, I --
Who else was playing tenor. Was Stump Evans --
No, Stump never did get to New York.
No, but I mean I'm thinking more or less in the chronological order of the way this thing came out, so I mean we'll say Hawk's first. Now then you and Prince.
Then was Benny Waters, [without] taking his place. He came in from Maryland, Baltimore, to New York, and he was working down at -- He's still in Paris now doing good. He was -- came to --
But he was never really much of a soloist. He usually --
Yeah, he was a good soloist.
Was he? But I mean --
Yes, he was. He didn't care about nobody.
Well, I always thought he was like a section man in those days.
Yeah, he played good section, (unintelligible). I tried to -- he tried to catch me in
from Paris and went to Jutland

Copenhagen because he came in (unintelligible), which is down on the other side, which is part of Copenhagen, in Denmark anyway. And Buddy Tate was there at the same time, and Bud and I could not run across (unintelligible) because when I was in Sweden Bud was back in Copenhagen. And then the promoter's girlfriend and his mother were born in Jutland (unintelligible). So when she came back one time for the weekend and her girlfriend and some of her relatives, (unintelligible) says, well, we saw Benny Waters advertised in the Copenhagen paper, (unintelligible), the Danish paper.

And he was in Jutland, so he sent word for me to come out there, but I was almost on the closing end of this concert thing, and we were going to Norway, and we went to Sweden and back there and we back there for some taping.
Well, what year -- you must get this on there. What year was it that you went to Denmark? Last year?
Last year, 1965, September --
Five -- and you went alone, and you played with -- groups in Scandinavia.
(Simultaneous remarks)
Well, that's marvelous.
I enjoyed it too. And they put me
pedestal way up on the top. They said, we just love you, the way you're playing. You just surprise everybody. Everybody took me and said --
(Unintelligible). Well, just going back to this sort of order of tenor players again. Now, all those Texas people -- I mean like the Budd Johnsons and --
Buddy Tate --
-- Buddy Tate, now they come up there because -- and Herschel Evans.
Herschel Evans.
Now, they must be coming up about 1930 or so.
They came after us, yes. Ben came there before --
No, Ben came after, because --
That's right.
-- he was playing piano when Budd Johnson first heard him.
That's right, played piano in the theater there.
Yeah. So, yeah, then like Illinois Arnett could one later and (unintelligible) still. But Chu was coming -- Chu must have come in almost next, I guess.
Let me see. When Chu, Billie Holiday and Teddy Wilson playing at a place called still there, called
the Hot Cha, but he had an upstairs to it, the -- that's where they were playing. (Unintelligible) was on tenor then. That's before he ever made a big name.

That's right. Ben, the next place they were playing, down to a place called the Wellworth Tavern on 126th Street and Seventh Avenue -- just torn down now -- big place, big room back there, cabaret; that's with Ben, Teddy Wilson, Billie Holiday singing. I forgot who the drummer was back there, but four pieces. He was playing tenor then after he left --
Well, there was a place, though, up there where I heard Billie -- '37, Harlem -- I don't know what they called that. She was singing with a club up there, some old club. That was 37 --
37 -- 37th Street?

Well, one was the Hot Cha, but the bar is still there now. It's still there, but the (unintelligible) part, they tore that out. They played upstairs there. Billy did the singing. Chu, Teddy Wilson -- she was the vocalist. I forgot who was on the drum, three pieces.
So Chu was on tenor then?
Chu was on tenor then. Yeah.
Well, no, I guess -- I guess from
what you say then that Chu actually does not follow you and all of them. I mean some of those Texas people must have been before him.
Let me see now. When Earl Hines came here, Bud Johnson was with Earl Hines' band, and—
Well, I mean Bud had been gone a long time before he got with Earl (unintelligible).
Yeah, I think Chu was before them fellows.
You think so?

Yeah, because now when Lester came in, Lester came in -- Lester was supposed to go with Fletcher, and then Ben went with Fletcher. Ben didn't have -- those guys was funny -- [Bird] (unintelligible) didn't impress me nothing. Lester -- kind of like a showmanship, you know -- and Lester walk up, set his horn on his shoulder, you know, (unintelligible). So Ben came and said to me, said, look at that son of a bitch over there, going up Seventh Avenue with that horn on his --
Oh, walking up the street?
Yeah.
Who said this to you, Ben --
Ben Webster. Ben didn't like him.
No?
See, what happened, before Hawk came

back from Europe, Lester was here. See, he came here to join Fletcher's band. He came and so did Ben. Ben came in earlier than Lester. And everybody was talking about this thing, you know, and naturally Lester take it to heart and Ben --and Ben couldn't take it. Hap, I ought to go over there and punch that so and so and so on in the mouth. Look at that.
I said, Ben, let him alone. Nothing you can do with him.
Do you think it had anything to do with the fact that Lester's sort of manner was a bit effeminate or anything?
Well, you know, he carried that way, but he actually wasn't that [sissy,] was he?
No, I know he wasn't. But I mean some people might have thought he was queer.

They could have. We had a nightclub called the Band Box for all the bands, musicians come in there, white and colored. So when Hawk came in town, he looked for me. I was playing (unintelligible), said, Ben said (unintelligible) to me, he said, hey, Hap, said, Hawk's in town (unintelligible). I said, yeah, we want to have a little party down at the club because (I was a member-part owner of the club. And (unintelligible) --
Oh, wait a minute. I better just put this on.
(Side 11)
I'd go down and listen to him.
Well, yeah, Hawk comes back from Europe, right?
Right. And that's when after (unintelligible) he made that "Body and Soul" because he had the big band.

So we said, I said, Ben, we're going to have a little party for Hawk on his return back to the States. Dan Byas and all (unintelligible) be there and Ben come, and, well, I said, Lester going to be there. You know, I ought to punch that so and so in his mouth. I said, Ben, don't come down and break up the joint, said don't pay it no mind. So Lester came in here, and Lester's (unintelligible) that's going to play, down, lot of the fellows, different bands downtown, why, they'd come and they'd play. They cut Basie's half - (unintelligible)
(Laughter)

So he had to get between Ben -- I said, Ben, let him alone. Don't bother him. Go on and play. He said, I'm going to take his horn and shove it down his damn throat. I said, oh, boy. I said (unintelligible), come on and have a little taste. So they had a battle of jazz. Basie's band and Hawk's band -- see, Hawk had this big band. After that's how he made this "Body and Soul" at the Golden Gate Ballroom, which is about two blocks --
What was the other band? Hawk's
band and --
Hawk had his big band then after he came back from Europe because that's when he made --
(Simultaneous remarks)
Count Basie.
Oh, Basie. I got you.

Basie, see -- Lester was with Basie. Now, everybody -- musicians going to go and see this thing, you know. So Ben said, Hap, hey, where you going? I said, let's go up there and hear the battle between Basie and Hawk. Yeah. All right. I'll pick you up. He had a car, you know. Pick you up -- I said okay. Well, man, (unintelligible) trump that bastard (unintelligible).
(Laughter)

I said, well, I said, guy's all right. But, Hap, so and so and so and so. I said, I go along with him, though. Pacify him. So they played together up there, band played. Hawk played -- a fast tune. Oh, man, he did about six choruses. That was the end of it. House (unintelligible) came in. Ben said, I told you, Hap. I said, that was the man trying to fill the big man's shoe. That satisfied Ben, because Hawk would have ate it up that night, because he knew a little -- you know, that's the end. And Hawk didn't hate Lester, but Hawk was going to prove, and that's what he did. And that did that's all Ben wanted he'd -- Hawk didn't want it. I told you I'd kill that bum.
(Laughter)

But (unintelligible) -- you know, when you -- you know, when you think back to all this business of tone and everything, well, I mean something that had to do with the fact that they were playing in these ballrooms where you wanted to produce a big sound.
Where you wanted -- right.
I know, I mean -- whereas the kind of tone Lester had, if he wasn't miked, I mean you couldn't hear him.--
That's true.
-- five yards away.
That's true. They had mikes (unintelligible) two big bandstands.
Well, what -- I mean what did you think of Lester when you first heard him?

Well, it was a peculiar style, and, you know, you always listen -- what the fellow's doing and what he's trying to do, like I never could fathom out what Coltrane wanted to do. I don't think he ever completed what he wanted to do.
Coltrane?
Right. I've dug him -- when he used to come down to Small's and sit back up there and play, and seemed like he was always reaching for something or trying to

do something that he hadn't -- what he hadn't wanted -- what he hadn't accomplished. And I listened to him time and time again. And I talked with him. I liked things he did. He was always moving on his horn, but it seemed like the man was always like reaching for something.
(Simultaneous remarks)
It was also that, I think, what was -- when you heard those long things where he played for 15, 20 minutes, I mean it was an awful lot of repetition.
Yeah, it was. Yeah.
And I mean maybe you're just sort of, as you say, you're searching, but I mean a lot of that stuff really sounds like what you would do at home.
It's true.
You know?
That's true.
Where you're trying to work something out, but you don't do it in public or on a record.

No, because I've found out two things Stanley (unintelligible) that, what the guys used to say to (unintelligible) me, said, you know, you a funny man with the horn. I said why. Said, we hear you play one night the same thing, and we go back the next night you don't -- what, did you forget what you played the night before? I says, I don't remember what I played the day before, because I'm always thinking about something else.

And Hawks said, well, you create as you go along, don't you? I said, well, maybe that's what you call it. But like he wrote in that book about those nine different choruses. I wasn't there and practicing on nine different choruses. I made the -- made two or three bars like so. Forget about it.
But when you get on -- the band is behind you, and you get that feeling, and they create.

Well, I take it, though, that if you -- I mean if you had an arrangement for a band and you played with this band every night, and you also have to fit that arrangement, then your solo is going to become rather the same every night.
It will because you are accustomed to playing it, and it comes.
I mean you've got --
(Simultaneous remarks)
You know you've got to make it fit with the --
Right.

-- what the -- when the brass is -- well, that's one thing, but if you play for, say, you know, some jump number with a totally different band six nights running, you'd probably take a different solo (unintelligible).
Oh, that's what happened with me over there in Copenhagen, because they'd ask you. I'd say
anything you fellows want to play. Well, they'd play all them swing tunes, this and that, ballads (unintelligible). It was real nice with me.

How much does tempo affect you? I mean, you know, if you were accustomed to playing a tune like you were playing on the -- at a certain tempo, and somebody hits it off much faster, I mean that changes what you play considerably, doesn't it?

Yes, it does, yeah. Changes the whole aspect of what you want to play, change it all the way around. I used to play (unintelligible) Body and Soul, three or four choruses as a ballad. Then we pick it up in two/four, fast two/four. But I quit doing it. Not that I didn't want to do it, but Charlie Ventura (unintelligible) tell me, he says, come here and listen. Said, why do you play it with the bell (unintelligible) play it in an even swing tempo? And so that's (the way) (unintelligible) wanted to do it. So I just it every night follow suit. But like you say, Stanley, you play the light and it becomes monotonous to you.
Well, that's right. You can't help that. I mean that's impossible, but I think that there's another thing that has changed. You know those tempos used to be --
That's right.
Those tempos used to be right to make
people want to dance.
Want to dance, yes.
Well, now you're no longer thinking like that. You're thinking entirely in terms of what will dazzle these people sitting at those tables with their beers.
Right. That's the main thing.
It's a totally different --
Totally different story. That's right.
Yeah. Well, I had no idea (unintelligible) it was 11, we made it 11?
Oh, sure.
See, we started at 2:30.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
