segments.chapter: Chicago childhood and learning clarinet
segments.title: How Albert Caldwell got the nickname Happy
segments.summary: Caldwell explains he learned to drive cars as a kid around a garage; the garage owner, a violinist and arranger, named him Happy.

segments.chapter: Chicago childhood and learning clarinet
segments.title: Parents, siblings and the piano at home
segments.summary: His sisters took piano and Lil Armstrong visited the house; his father played banjo; he is the youngest of seven; no other sibling became a professional.

segments.chapter: Chicago childhood and learning clarinet
segments.title: Following parade clarinets and the Wendell Phillips High School crowd
segments.summary: He loved the clarinet, followed parade bands with Omer Simeon, and names famous alumni of Wendell Phillips High School.

segments.chapter: Chicago childhood and learning clarinet
segments.title: First clarinet lessons: the high school bandmaster and Buster Bailey
segments.summary: Started clarinet in the high school band under Professor Tulesty; his distant cousin Buster Bailey, working with Erskine Tate, gave him lessons.

segments.chapter: Chicago childhood and learning clarinet
segments.title: Sitting in at the Sunset and copying Buster Bailey's solo
segments.summary: He sat in at the Sunset Cafe and played Buster Bailey's 'Tootsie Goodbye' solo note for note, to Rudy Jackson's amusement; the band was Carroll Dickerson's.

segments.chapter: Chicago childhood and learning clarinet
segments.title: The Simeon brothers and the Chicago cabarets young clarinetists haunted
segments.summary: Omer Simeon started clarinet in Chicago; the young clarinet players went to the Royal Garden, Dreamland and other cabarets to hear Oliver, Noone and others.

segments.chapter: Chicago childhood and learning clarinet
segments.title: Darnell Howard, Benny Carter and John Chilton's book
segments.summary: He admired the Chicago clarinet style of Darnell Howard and learned from Chilton's book that Howard and Benny Carter were cousins.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: The 8th Illinois National Guard band at about sixteen
segments.summary: He joined the 370th Eighth Illinois Infantry National Guard band, stationed in Chicago, and got good reading and concert training.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Playing jazz gigs in East Chicago, Indiana
segments.summary: His first work was a small group playing night gigs and holidays in East Chicago, riding the Illinois Central and passing the hat.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Columbia Tavern at 31st and State, and Louis Armstrong stopping by
segments.summary: He joined Bernie Young's band at the Columbia Tavern; Louis Armstrong dropped in to hear the five-piece group.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Who was in the Columbia Tavern band: McKendrick and Dolly Jones's family
segments.summary: Personnel included guitarist Mike McKendrick, Dolly's mother on trumpet and her uncle Turk on drums; nobody recalls Dolly's surname.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Dolly's father was Lonnie Johnson, and a Jelly Roll aside
segments.summary: Caldwell reveals Dolly's father was the blues guitarist and singer Lonnie Johnson, which leads to talk of Jelly Roll Morton's wife and mistress.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Dolly's mother and Turk as show-band readers
segments.summary: Dolly sat in; her mother and uncle were strong sight readers from circus, shows and the Monogram Theater.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Leaving the Tavern band for Bernie Young; Dolly Jones as leader
segments.summary: Bernie Young organised his own recording band and Caldwell left the Tavern, whose band belonged to trumpeter Dolly Jones.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Bobby Williams, the trumpeter who sounded like Roy Eldridge
segments.summary: After Dolly left they used a young trumpeter and a Louisville drummer; Caldwell praises Bobby Williams of the Sunset and the way older players encouraged youngsters.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Cecil Irwin, Morehouse and Wilberforce
segments.summary: Caldwell and Cecil Irwin planned to attend college together but parents sent Irwin to Morehouse and Caldwell to Wilberforce.

segments.chapter: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
segments.title: Albert system versus Boehm system clarinet
segments.summary: He stayed with the Albert system clarinet, which he thought allowed free passages and a distinct tone that the Boehm could not.

segments.chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
segments.title: Buying a first saxophone and leaving it with Johnny Dodds
segments.summary: Clarinet devotees disliked the saxophone; he left his first alto with Johnny Dodds before leaving Chicago for New York.

segments.chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
segments.title: Meeting Coleman Hawkins and Hawk's cello and clarinet
segments.summary: Hawkins heard Caldwell's clarinet style in Chicago and invited him to join; they discuss Hawkins's cello training and why Caldwell settled on tenor.

segments.chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
segments.title: Bernie Young at the Wisconsin Roof Garden
segments.summary: He played about six months in Wisconsin and later at the Wisconsin Roof Garden, a hotel job that lasted several years; he was in Newark with Rex Stewart when they sent for him.

segments.chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
segments.title: The 1923 Bernie Young recording and Stump Evans's C-melody
segments.summary: Personnel of the 1923 record; Stump Evans, from Kansas City, played C-melody, which people mistook for alto, and Hawkins asked about him.

segments.chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
segments.title: Frankie Trumbauer, C-melody and keeping one's own style
segments.summary: He remarks on the C-melody saxophone, Trumbauer's advice to stay on tenor and Hawkins praising his independence from others' influence.

segments.chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
segments.title: Alto players who switched to tenor and Caldwell's doubling
segments.summary: Discussion of Lester Young and others who began on alto; Caldwell doubled tenor and baritone with Arthur Gibbs's band and could pick up alto.

segments.chapter: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
segments.title: Picking the clarinet up again; Prince Robinson
segments.summary: He estimates four months to get back on clarinet; Dance recalls Prince Robinson sounding rusty on a recording, and Caldwell recalls him doubling with Snowden.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Joining Mamie Smith's band in Chicago
segments.summary: Back from Wisconsin, he joined Mamie Smith through a drummer, Clifford Jones nicknamed Guy Wattle.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Drummer Frank Andrew, nicknamed Jew Baby
segments.summary: A drummer in the group whose father played drums at the Lincoln Theater where Fats Waller played organ.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Mamie Smith's theater circuit and TOBA
segments.summary: The band played colored theaters in Cleveland, Detroit, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington on the TOBA circuit.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Mamie Smith compared with Bessie, Clara and Trixie Smith
segments.summary: Mamie was a smooth vaudeville singer who looked the part, not a blues shouter, and her fame owed to the first record and her agent.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Leaving Mamie Smith and the salary
segments.summary: He left in February 1924, stayed in New York, and says they were paid well.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Mamie Smith band personnel: Harvey Brooks, Joe Smith, Bob Fuller
segments.summary: Players he recalls: pianist Harvey Brooks, trumpeter Joe Smith, violinist Henry Sapero, Cecil Carpenter and clarinetist Bob Fuller.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Bob Fuller: dance school, jail turnkey and clarinet limits
segments.summary: Bob Fuller later worked at the Dreamland Dance School and became a city jail turnkey; Dance and Caldwell judge his clarinet amateurish.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Dance schools and society bands: Happy Roark and Lucky Roberts
segments.summary: After Mamie he worked dance schools and large society dance bands, which paid well.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Summer at Asbury Park and Bobby Brown in Newark
segments.summary: He and Walter Johnson commuted to Newark and worked with saxophonist Bobby Brown, who left music for a restaurant.

segments.chapter: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
segments.title: Walter Johnson and the Friendly Fifty club
segments.summary: Walter Johnson, a New York drummer, was at the dance school; Caldwell describes the Friendly Fifty club of veteran musicians.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Cliff Jackson takes over the Nest Club band from Snowden
segments.summary: Snowden moved to the Bandville Club and gave his Nest Club job to Cliff Jackson, whose band Caldwell joined and named A Bunch of Keys.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Tricking trumpeters by playing in hard keys
segments.summary: The Carter and Jackson crowd tested a newcomer at the dance corner by playing through every key.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: New York versus Chicago jazz in the twenties
segments.summary: Dance and Caldwell agree New York records of the 1920s were stiffer than Chicago's though New York musicians read better.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: King Oliver and Louis Armstrong's second-trumpet breaks
segments.summary: Caldwell watched Oliver's band and how Armstrong improvised a perfect second part in the two-trumpet breaks.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Casino Simpson and the Chicago pianists before Earl Hines
segments.summary: Chicago was big after Caldwell left; Casino Simpson, a Wilberforce classmate, imitated Fats Waller and Earl Hines.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Teddy Weatherford and Glover Compton
segments.summary: Caldwell doubts Earl Hines copied Teddy Weatherford; Glover Compton was more an entertainer at the piano.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton as a talker and comedian
segments.summary: Jelly Roll held court on a Harlem corner outside the Rhythm Club and could talk himself into and out of a job.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Rehearsals and the Apollo Theater audition with Jelly Roll
segments.summary: Caldwell recalls rehearsals and an audition for Mr. Schiffman at the Apollo where Jelly Roll insisted on playing his new number and lost the job.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Finger Buster and Don't You Leave Me Here
segments.summary: Discussion of Jelly Roll's tunes, including one Caldwell did not know he composed until reading about it in Denmark.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: A second audition ruined by Jelly Roll and the song plugger
segments.summary: At an audition near Roseland, Jelly Roll recognised the promoter, a former song plugger, and insulted him about his fur coat.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Jelly Roll's character and the Princeton prom
segments.summary: Dance and Caldwell on Jelly's braggadocio and kindness; at a Princeton June prom Jelly Roll announced himself as king of jazz to students.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Jelly Roll the composer and his last recording band
segments.summary: Jelly Roll's compositions were advanced; Caldwell lists the New Orleans players on the last recording.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Jelly Roll's death, his relatives and the question of his birthplace
segments.summary: After a settlement with RCA Jelly left for California; friends searched for relatives and Caldwell debates whether he was born in New Orleans or Birmingham.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: Cliff Jackson's band at the Nest and the long-haired professor pianist
segments.summary: Personnel at the Nest and the pianist they called the Professor, who read everything and later went to Europe.

segments.chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
segments.title: The Nest Club and Harlem's Seventh Avenue clubs
segments.summary: The Nest was off Seventh Avenue at 133rd Street amid Tillie's Chicken Shack, Small's and other clubs.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Snowden, gigging and joining Charlie Johnson at Small's Paradise
segments.summary: After Snowden he gigged until joining Charlie Johnson's summer replacement band at Small's in 1926 while Johnson was in Atlantic City.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Water in the baritone and the Small's personnel
segments.summary: A prank in which water was put in a baritone saxophone, and a list of the band members.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Willie Gant, an overlooked stride pianist
segments.summary: Willie Gant never recorded much, played cocktail piano at Rudy's, and was a stride player in the class of Fats and Willie the Lion.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Reuben's place and the cutting contests
segments.summary: The Harlem pianists held cutting contests at Reuben's on 130th Street, attended by Fats, the Lion, Basie, Tatum and Donald Lambert.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Willie Gant's band and the aftermath of Johnson's return
segments.summary: Gant's 1926 band was very good, but the group dissolved when Charlie Johnson returned.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Playing in the Village for gangsters
segments.summary: He worked Greenwich Village bands where gangsters ran the clubs.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Giving up clarinet for tenor; doubling clarinet and soprano
segments.summary: He stopped playing clarinet as a feature when he stayed on tenor with Cliff Jackson, though section parts required clarinet and soprano.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Pipe and straight soprano saxophones; Hodges and Bechet
segments.summary: There are two kinds of soprano sax; Hodges played it like Bechet and shared Caldwell's birthday.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Charlie Holmes, Duke Ellington and lip trouble
segments.summary: Charlie Holmes would not join Ellington after Hodges left; Dance and Caldwell talk about his refusing to record and lip problems.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Charlie Holmes's failing eye and refusing to record
segments.summary: Caldwell tries to coax Holmes out to recordings, thinks his eye trouble keeps him home, and compares Art Tatum.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Recording with Thomas Morris in 1926
segments.summary: Caldwell recalls Thomas Morris, uncle of Marlowe Morris, the 1926 electrical recordings and Morris's later turn to Father Divine's church.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Ward Pinkett as friend and roommate
segments.summary: Caldwell and Ward Pinkett were buddies; Pinkett was a nice trumpeter of part Indian descent who stayed with the group.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Ward Pinkett's death in 1937
segments.summary: Pinkett, who had worked with Jelly Roll, died after a fall into a flooded basement while Caldwell was away on the road with Jesse Owens's band.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Indian ancestry in jazz musicians
segments.summary: Caldwell and Dance discuss Native American heritage among musicians and in the South, citing Pettiford, Fats Navarro and his own grandfather.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Colored, Negro, Black, and Caldwell's mixed family
segments.summary: They discuss changing racial terms and Caldwell says his Welsh-named mother's family looked white while his sister was dark.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Mixed ancestry and doubts about African origins theories
segments.summary: They discuss ethnic mixture in England and America and doubt generalised theories about African origins of jazz.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: The spelling of Caldwell
segments.summary: His name was sometimes spelled with a u; teachers misspelled it.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Charlie Johnson's band personnel
segments.summary: He returned to Charlie Johnson for about a year with Jimmy Harris, Tommy Ladnier, Benny Carter, Benny Waters and others.

segments.chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
segments.title: Tommy Ladnier's retreat from music
segments.summary: Ladnier, like Ward Pinkett, withdrew from music, and Caldwell thinks Hawkins had the same disgust.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Pay in 1926 and civil service afterwards
segments.summary: Dance and Caldwell compare 1926 wages with later pay; Caldwell joined civil service after the war and ran a duplicating room at City College.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson musicians' high salaries
segments.summary: Benny Morton's story shows Fletcher Henderson's band paid exceptionally well.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Substituting for Coleman Hawkins in Fletcher Henderson's band
segments.summary: When Hawkins went off driving in his car, Caldwell pinch hit for him and found the salary fantastic.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Fletcher's Roseland band, Joe Smith and Howard Scott
segments.summary: He lists men in Fletcher Henderson's Roseland band and admires Joe Smith's muted style, shared only by Howard Scott.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Hanging out with Joe Smith and Bubber Miley; Howard Scott
segments.summary: They gathered uptown after work; Howard Scott later left music for the post office and Dance wants to contact him.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Howard Scott leaves music for a day job
segments.summary: Scott drank heavily, took a day job as gig work slackened, and played society-type bands after Fletcher.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Bubber Miley versus Joe Smith, and the Smith brothers
segments.summary: Miley's wa-wa mute covered a poor open tone, Charlie Irvis used a mute on trombone, and Joe, Luke and Russell Smith are compared.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Hawkins's criticism of Russell Smith's lead playing
segments.summary: Dance says Hawkins faulted Russell Smith's lead trumpet and Fletcher's loss of Cootie Williams; Caldwell notes Hawk seldom criticized.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Drinks with Coleman Hawkins at the White Rose on 52nd Street
segments.summary: Hawkins, who never bought drinks for others, bought Caldwell drinks and urged him to keep his own style.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Hawkins as master of the tenor, with Caldwell and Prince Robinson
segments.summary: Among early tenor players the three to get by were Hawk, Happy and Prince Robinson; Hawkins was master of slap tongue before dropping it.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson at the Club Bandville and Broadway Jones
segments.summary: Fletcher led the band at the Bandville on 129th Street under Broadway Jones's name; Jones was an entertainer who sang big show songs at society gigs.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Lois Deppe, the Great Day show and his fall from the top
segments.summary: Dance recalls singer Lois Deppe's career and the show Great Day, which Show Boat overshadowed, and his later life in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Stump Evans falls ill, and Cab Calloway wanted Caldwell on alto
segments.summary: Caldwell recommended Stump Evans to Cab but Evans got sick; he had left him on C-melody.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Louis Armstrong with Fletcher Henderson in New York
segments.summary: Caldwell went to hear Armstrong with Fletcher, who recorded King Porter Stomp; Armstrong stayed about a year then returned to Chicago.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Could Louis Armstrong read? Erskine Tate's Vendome pit band
segments.summary: They discuss the reading demands of theater pit work with Erskine Tate and doubt a story about Armstrong's music being marked.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Learning to read clarinet parts; Darnell Howard on three instruments
segments.summary: Caldwell explains how parts are learned in a school band; Darnell Howard played violin, trumpet and clarinet.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Multi-instrumentalists: George Dixon and doublers who play many horns
segments.summary: Dixon played alto and baritone beautifully; players who take up many horns rarely play any one well.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Coltrane on soprano and the difficulty of the straight soprano
segments.summary: Dance heard Coltrane's soprano as bagpipes; Caldwell and Hodges agree the straight soprano is hard to play.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Running the changes versus creating on a solo
segments.summary: Caldwell tells students not to just run notes and says he creates as he goes, never repeating a solo.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Hawkins refusing Body and Soul; playing the same hits nightly
segments.summary: Dance and Caldwell discuss how musicians tire of audience requests for their hits, such as Hawkins and Body and Soul or Hodges and Carney.

segments.chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
segments.title: Keep Shuffling revue and Eubie Blake
segments.summary: Caldwell was briefly in the Keep Shuffling revue, which ran about two years; Eubie Blake is a fellow lodge member and Caldwell joined the lodge in 1946.

segments.chapter: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
segments.title: Arthur Gibbs's band at the Savoy and Colonnades: personnel
segments.summary: Caldwell played tenor in Arthur Gibbs's ten-piece band, with Billy Taylor, Sammy Hodges and Edgar Sampson; Gibbs wrote Running Wild.

segments.chapter: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
segments.title: Arrangers and Chick Webb's band as the other Savoy house band
segments.summary: Sammy Hodges and others arranged; Chick Webb's band on the other bandstand included Elmer Williams, Johnny Hodges and Cuffe.

segments.chapter: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
segments.title: Savoy house bands, Fess Williams and Edgar Sampson
segments.summary: They split the Savoy with Chick Webb in 1927-28, moved to the Colonnades in 1929; Sampson later arranged for Chick, Duke and Fletcher.

segments.chapter: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
segments.title: Recording Knocking the Jug with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: With Jack Teagarden and Kaiser Marshall, an unwritten blues session produced Knocking the Jug and Muggles.

segments.chapter: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
segments.title: How studio sessions were run and the morning call
segments.summary: Sessions were made up unwritten with several takes; musicians went to the Rhythm Club until the morning call.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Elmer Snowden's band at Small's, and Garvin Bushell's many instruments
segments.summary: Snowden picked good players; Garvin Bushell, first seen in Chicago with Lucille Hegamin, played oboe, flute and bassoon and the band played overture excerpts at intermission.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: The saxophone as the bastard instrument and classical saxophonists
segments.summary: Caldwell recalls old masters calling the saxophone a bastard instrument, and discusses Rudy Wiedoft and recitalists; Dance dislikes the classical sound.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: What Hawkins showed the tenor could do: depth, tone and running changes
segments.summary: They contrast Hawkins's full tenor tone with light modern players who run changes without telling a story.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Back with Charlie Johnson at Small's, and leaving a band properly
segments.summary: Off and on 18 months to two years; musicians took weeks off for other gigs and Caldwell never left a band cold.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: The Elite Serenaders and Roy Eldridge arrive at Small's
segments.summary: The Elite Serenaders from Pittsburgh, with Roy Eldridge and his brother, came to Small's in 1926 while Charlie Johnson was in Atlantic City.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Wilberforce, Jimmy Rushing and Caldwell's father
segments.summary: Caldwell was at Wilberforce years before Horace Henderson and Rushing, left before graduating, and says his father worked for an elevator company.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Covering for Hawkins in Fletcher's band while with Arthur Gibbs
segments.summary: Hawk would leave when Fletcher came in; Caldwell played sets with Gibbs and Fletcher at the Savoy and Roseland and got two pays.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's difficult arrangements and Charlie Dixon's hard keys
segments.summary: Arrangements by Don Redman and Charlie Dixon were in hard keys; Fletcher wrote easier ones, and the early ones were rough.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Don Redman as an exacting, gentlemanly arranger
segments.summary: Don Redman graduated in music, played ocarina, led a band that drove Sidney DeParis's lips hard, and was always a gentleman.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Brothers who could not get along in bands
segments.summary: Caldwell lists band brothers such as Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey, the White brothers and the McRaes who quarrelled.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Horace Henderson's treatment of Fletcher, and his absence at the funeral
segments.summary: Horace borrowed Fletcher's car, took his music and was missing at the funeral; Dance later found him playing a hotel lounge in Colorado.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: Marlowe Morris, John Hammond and a pianist who never showed up
segments.summary: Marlowe Morris had a trio at Small's but was irresponsible and later became an alcoholic despite Hammond's help.

segments.chapter: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
segments.title: John Hammond's quiet kindnesses
segments.summary: Dance recounts Hammond paying Sandy Williams's dentist; Caldwell says Marlowe could have gone far had he listened.

segments.chapter: Vernon Andrade's band and Harlem life
segments.title: Vernon Andrade's house band at the Renaissance Casino
segments.summary: Caldwell played Thursday through Sunday with Andrade at the Renaissance, with a regular personnel and arrangements copied from Duke records.

segments.chapter: Vernon Andrade's band and Harlem life
segments.title: Andrade's band outplays Cab Calloway at the Savoy
segments.summary: Andrade's band was booked at the Savoy; one night they were so good Cab's band could not get back on the stand.

segments.chapter: Vernon Andrade's band and Harlem life
segments.title: Vernon Andrade from Panama and his island musicians
segments.summary: Andrade was a quiet, businesslike Panamanian; the band included men from the islands, Zutty and Louie Metcalf.

segments.chapter: Vernon Andrade's band and Harlem life
segments.title: Colonel Julian, the Black Eagle
segments.summary: A side story about Colonel Julian and the aviators' acts, and a fight Claude Hopkins had with Cab Calloway.

segments.chapter: Vernon Andrade's band and Harlem life
segments.title: Marriage, the Rhythm Club newsletter and writing
segments.summary: Caldwell was married and separated, assistant secretary at the Rhythm Club, and wrote articles for its little book.

segments.chapter: Tiny Bradshaw and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.title: Meeting Tiny Bradshaw and joining his new band
segments.summary: Caldwell first saw Tiny singing and drumming in a joint while with Danny Logan, and joined his band in 1934 as assistant bandleader.

segments.chapter: Tiny Bradshaw and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.title: Assistant bandleader: warming up the brass, and band personnel
segments.summary: Caldwell opened shows with head numbers to warm up the brass, and lists a big band with George Mathews and Mack Madison.

segments.chapter: Tiny Bradshaw and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald joins Tiny Bradshaw after the Harlem Opera House contest
segments.summary: After winning the amateur contest Ella sang with Bradshaw's band, then went back to Chick Webb without a contract.

segments.chapter: Tiny Bradshaw and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.title: Chick Webb's band after Ella Fitzgerald
segments.summary: Dance and Caldwell consider Edgar Sampson versus Al Feldman and say Webb's band was a commercial group.

segments.chapter: Tiny Bradshaw and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald stops the show and Caldwell's advice
segments.summary: Ella, put on last, took encores; Caldwell encouraged her backstage and warned her about stage-door Johnnies.

segments.chapter: Tiny Bradshaw and Ella Fitzgerald
segments.title: Dinah Washington gambling before her show
segments.summary: Caldwell recalls Dinah Washington as the toughest singer and gambling when she should have been ready.

segments.chapter: Louis Metcalf and leading his own bands
segments.title: Playing with Louis Metcalf's small group and Vernon Andrade
segments.summary: Metcalf formed a group for the Savoy and the Village, then Andrade picked them; Metcalf set up the entertainment routines.

segments.chapter: Louis Metcalf and leading his own bands
segments.title: Leading bands for Masonic balls and giving sidemen solos
segments.summary: Through the Masonic fraternity he led groups from four to sixteen pieces, using stock arrangements and letting every man take solos.

segments.chapter: Louis Metcalf and leading his own bands
segments.title: His feature numbers and the leader as announcer
segments.summary: He featured ballads such as Stardust and swing choruses, and acted as announcer who let the soloists do their thing.

segments.chapter: Louis Metcalf and leading his own bands
segments.title: Stretch Carl Ridley and why he gives soloists room
segments.summary: Caldwell praised young tenor Carl Ridley, said many good players stay hidden, and explained he prefers to feature his men.

segments.chapter: Louis Metcalf and leading his own bands
segments.title: Break for coffee, Side Seven
segments.summary: The interviewers decide to continue; two hours more are left.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Rehearsing next door to Jelly Roll, Lips Page, and the Danish record
segments.summary: Jelly lived at 131st Street next to where the group rehearsed; Caldwell also toured with Lips Page in 1945 and received a Danish record of the Morton album.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: The Jelly Roll Morton sessions: personnel and arrangements
segments.summary: Personnel included Bechet, Albert Nicholas, Sidney DeParis and Zutty Singleton; Jelly wrote out the arrangements for his numbers.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Tunes recorded: Ride, High Society, Winin' Boy
segments.summary: Caldwell and Dance run through the repertoire of the Morton sessions.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Trombonist Fred Robinson and a possible Willie Gant record
segments.summary: Fred Robinson, who had recorded with Jelly in Chicago, worked on the subway and retired to Cleveland; a Chilton listing of a Gant record puzzles them.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Opening Minton's Playhouse with Henry Minton
segments.summary: As Henry Minton, the first black delegate in Local 802, opened the Playhouse, Caldwell put in a group with Pop Foster, Andy Anderson and pianist Babe Salters.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Jam sessions at Minton's and the coming of bebop; Thelonious Monk
segments.summary: It was where Caldwell met Dizzy, Parker and Monk; he remembers Monk as a normal pianist who changed his style.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Alto player Swindell
segments.summary: Swindell, who lived next door to Charlie Parker, might have rivalled Parker had drugs not ruined him; he died after moving to the West Coast.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Club Baron, Clark Monroe's Uptown House and Minton's
segments.summary: Caldwell clarifies the Club Baron became Clark Monroe's Uptown House, which came after Minton's; the building later belonged to Roy Campanella.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Minton's as bebop center and reactions to the new music
segments.summary: Minton's drew young and middle-class listeners; Dance and Caldwell say bebop was unpopular at first and not the only direction jazz could take.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: Caldwell leaves Minton's after six months; Henry Minton's death
segments.summary: He left to go on the road, remembers banking for Minton, and says Minton died in 1969 and was buried by his lodge.

segments.chapter: The Jelly Roll Morton records and Minton's Playhouse
segments.title: The after-hours place underneath Minton's and the hotel above
segments.summary: A quieter after-hours joint was downstairs; the hotels above had apartments where liquor was sold.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Bardu Ali's band at the Club Paradise, Atlantic City, and Philadelphia
segments.summary: Bardu Ali fronted an eleven or twelve piece band for the Club Paradise season, then took a smaller band to Philadelphia.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Atlantic City clubs and the loss of gambling
segments.summary: They name the Club Paradise, Club Harlem and other places and regret Atlantic City's decline.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Hearing of Pearl Harbor in a Philadelphia hotel with Basie's men
segments.summary: Caldwell, Dickie Wells, Jimmy Rushing and Don Byas heard the news on the radio on an off Sunday.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Playing in Slappy's band at Pennsauken
segments.summary: Slappy led a six-piece band on the river across from Camden with Ken Pope on piano and Caldwell on tenor.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Charlie Gaines's band in Philadelphia and Club Harlem
segments.summary: After joining the Philadelphia union board Caldwell worked with Charlie Gaines in Philadelphia and at Club Harlem in Atlantic City.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Billy Douglas, the Connecticut trumpeter who left Earl Hines
segments.summary: Billy Douglas, an arranger from New Haven, was lost to drink when Earl Hines was leaving New York.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Billy Douglas sits in with Roy Eldridge and Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: At a Sunday jam session Douglas ran all the chords and impressed Roy Eldridge and the others.

segments.chapter: Philadelphia, Atlantic City and the war years
segments.title: Cuban Bennett gives Billy Douglas his horn
segments.summary: Cuban Bennett, Benny Carter's cousin, gave Douglas his old trumpet before working for Campbell Soup in Camden.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Benny Carter's dignified manner and the nickname King
segments.summary: Carter was always straightforward and dignified; Dickie Wells called him King because he played so much alto.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: How teaching changed Benny Carter and Cozy Cole's playing
segments.summary: Dance and Caldwell feel that musicians who teach for years lose some of their edge.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Teaching jazz at City College, and Paul Quinichette as a Lester Young copy
segments.summary: Caldwell tells students to find their own sound; Quinichette copies Lester Young well yet keeps some independence, like Ben Webster.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Ben Webster switches from a Conn to a Selmer saxophone
segments.summary: Caldwell coached Webster through the unfamiliar Selmer, whose tone carries farther than it sounds under the player's ear.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Why players moved to Selmer, and Caldwell's current horn
segments.summary: Most players switched to Selmer; Caldwell bought a new Selmer before the Denmark trip.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Metal and rubber mouthpieces
segments.summary: Caldwell never had mouthpiece trouble; the section with Arthur Gibbs began using metal mouthpieces in 1927 and Hawkins did too.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Tone, microphone technique and playing too loud
segments.summary: In Denmark teachers praised Caldwell's tone; he backs off the mike, and Dance cites Coltrane's loudness.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Hawkins's reeds and the development of his sound
segments.summary: Hawk used hard reeds, number three and a half or four; Dance feels his sound grew stronger over the years.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Meeting Hawkins at a Harlem supermarket
segments.summary: Caldwell last saw Hawk in uptown Harlem shopping for his family; Hilton Jefferson lived in the same building.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Hawkins's decline: vodka, the beard and rumours
segments.summary: Caldwell heard Hawkins was drinking two fifths a day and not eating; Charlie Holmes described him as an old man of the mountains.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Why Hawkins broke down and his eating
segments.summary: Dance thinks the Swiss girlfriend's departure broke him; they recall his weakness and former hearty appetite.

segments.chapter: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
segments.title: Diet, health and what people eat
segments.summary: Caldwell and Dance compare modern food rules with his long-lived father and discuss quitting smoking.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: Joining Masonry and the musicians in the lodge
segments.summary: Caldwell was a mason from 1946; Lem Johnson, the deacon of the blues, and others advanced through the degrees.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: Harlem Lodge Number Four masters and musician members
segments.summary: Caldwell was elected Master in 1949; he lists musician members and later masters such as Eubie Blake, Jonah Jones and Cozy Cole.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: Does Masonry help musicians' lives? Joppa Lodge and Harlem Lodge
segments.summary: Caldwell thinks the principles help; Hodges, Carney and Procope belonged to Joppa 55, and he served as a grand lodge officer in the 1960s.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: Dean of the study class and the work of a past master
segments.summary: Caldwell teaches new masons their degrees and urges past masters to stay active.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: Brotherhood, favoritism and the moral side of Masonry
segments.summary: They discuss helping a brother in the music business, church obligations and how Masonry teaches everyday morality.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: Masonic funerals and the funeral team
segments.summary: Caldwell describes the well-conducted masonic funerals and eleven funerals in 1959.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: New Orleans funerals as a gimmick
segments.summary: Dance and Caldwell say the New Orleans funeral band has become a gimmick, and that street funerals have faded in New York.

segments.chapter: Masonic lodge and musicians
segments.title: Ray Nance's long funeral and funeral services as shows
segments.summary: Dance recounts delivering a eulogy at Nance's two-hour funeral and they agree services should not be vaudeville shows.

segments.chapter: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
segments.title: Playing around New York as leader and sideman since 1946
segments.summary: After 1946 Caldwell played with his own groups and as a sideman, often at Bing's place.

segments.chapter: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
segments.title: Civil service job at City College
segments.summary: He passed civil service exams and worked at City College from November 1957, first in the mail room, improving a stencil card process.

segments.chapter: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
segments.title: Jazz seminars at City College and other colleges
segments.summary: About three years ago he began bringing small groups to college jazz seminars.

segments.chapter: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
segments.title: Trumpeter Bernard Flood
segments.summary: Flood worked with Louie Armstrong's style, plays gigs and is about to retire from his government job; Dance remarks on a shortage of old-school trumpeters.

segments.chapter: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
segments.title: Who plays in the seminar group and how a college seminar runs
segments.summary: Caldwell takes Gene Rodgers, Tommy Benford and others; they play, announce each soloist and answer students' questions.

segments.chapter: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
segments.title: Music Dial column and Philadelphia union board
segments.summary: In Philadelphia he wrote for Music Dial, served two years on the executive board of Local 274, and stays active with his day job and lodge.

segments.chapter: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
segments.title: Leaving Chicago in February 1924 in the cold
segments.summary: He left with Mamie Smith in bitter cold; they talk about Chicago winters.

segments.chapter: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
segments.title: Big Jim Colosimo's murder and the start of gangster Chicago
segments.summary: As a high school student working downtown he saw the beginnings of Capone's Mafia after Colosimo was assassinated; Prohibition did no harm to musicians' work.

segments.chapter: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
segments.title: Why Chicago led New York in cabarets and night life
segments.summary: Chicago was the cabaret center of the country around 1922, with a concentrated black population.

segments.chapter: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
segments.title: Map of the South Side cabarets: Dreamland, Sunset, Columbia Tavern
segments.summary: Caldwell lists the cabarets and after-hours places along State Street from 31st to 35th, and who led the bands.

segments.chapter: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
segments.title: Chicago's theaters: Vendome, Grand, Pekin, Regal
segments.summary: The Vendome was a former fraternal house with Erskine Tate's orchestra; the Grand showed vaudeville; the Regal was built later and torn down.

segments.chapter: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
segments.title: A black entertainment district and the white audience uptown
segments.summary: Entertainment was concentrated in a mostly black area from 31st to 47th Street, with ballrooms and armories, and white patrons came to the ritzier places as in Harlem.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Chu Berry picks up the tenor at the Colonnades
segments.summary: At the Colonnades with Fat Man Turner's Arcadians, Chu Berry filled in on tenor when the tenor player did not show and kept it.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Chu Berry's portrait at the Elks Home in Charleston, West Virginia
segments.summary: On tour with Tiny Bradshaw, Caldwell found Chu's picture at the Elks home, where knowing Chu meant free drinks.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Who influenced whom among early tenors: Hawk, Happy and Prince Robinson
segments.summary: Everyone heard Hawk first; Prince Robinson started at the Calvert Palace and was influenced by Hawk.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Bob Carroll and the rehearsal with Jesse Stone
segments.summary: Bob Carroll was a comical, outspoken tenor who clashed with Jesse Stone at a rehearsal for the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Ben Webster, Bob Dorsey and the three B's argument
segments.summary: Comedian Pigmeat asked Caldwell to settle an argument among Ben Webster, Bob Dorsey and Bob Carroll about Hawk.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Bob Carroll's street fight and his drinking
segments.summary: Caldwell recalls pulling Bob Carroll off a fight on Seventh Avenue; he drank enough to raise hell but was no alcoholic.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Benny Waters as a tenor soloist
segments.summary: They place Benny Waters, who came from Baltimore, in the order of early tenor players; Dance thinks he was a section man.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: The 1975 jazz concert tour of Denmark and Scandinavia
segments.summary: Caldwell toured Denmark, Sweden and Norway in September 1975 and missed Benny Waters and Buddy Tate, who were elsewhere.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: The Texas tenors, Chu Berry, Billie Holiday and Teddy Wilson at the Hot Cha
segments.summary: They sort the arrival of Texas tenors and recall Chu with Billie Holiday and Teddy Wilson at the Hot Cha and Wellworth Tavern.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Ben Webster resents Lester Young's arrival
segments.summary: Ben Webster disliked Lester Young's showmanship and walk up Seventh Avenue and threatened him; they discuss Lester's manner.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Welcome party for Hawk and the Hawkins-Basie battle
segments.summary: At a party after Hawkins returned from Europe, Ben wanted to fight Lester, but at the battle of the bands Hawk settled it with six choruses.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Lester Young's tone and John Coltrane searching on the horn
segments.summary: Dance says Lester's tone would not fill ballrooms without mikes; Caldwell found Coltrane always reaching for something.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Creating as you go and playing the same solo nightly
segments.summary: Caldwell does not remember what he played the night before; arranged parts repeat, while free numbers change each night, as in Copenhagen.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Tempo and dancing versus dazzling listeners
segments.summary: Tempo changes what a player plays; Caldwell dropped his fast Body and Soul; they contrast dance tempos with tempos for listeners at tables.

segments.chapter: Tenor saxophonists and closing reflections
segments.title: Closing the session
segments.summary: Dance notes the time, they started at 2:30, and the recording ends.
